--- title: "Census Data in Python, Part 1: The Census API with requests and Polars" subtitle: "ACS and decennial data for North Carolina counties and census tracts" description: "Call the Census API directly with requests, load the results into Polars, and build a reusable function for pulling ACS and decennial data." order: 4 --- ::: {.callout-note} ## About this tutorial **Time:** about 30 minutes. **Prerequisites:** Python 3.10 or newer, basic familiarity with data frames, and a Census API key. If you haven't read [Census 101](census-101.qmd) yet, skim it first. By the end, you will be able to: - store your Census API key safely - read and build a Census API request URL - load API results into a Polars DataFrame and clean them - write a reusable function for pulling census data - pull ACS data for counties and census tracts, and 2020 decennial data - find the variable IDs you need ::: ## Why talk to the API directly? R users have [tidycensus](census-r-part1.qmd), which hides the Census API behind friendly functions. Python has no package that plays the same role quite as smoothly. The good news is that the API itself is simple. A request is just a URL, and the response is just a table in JSON format. Once you understand the pieces, a short function gives you most of what tidycensus offers. This tutorial uses three libraries: - [requests](https://requests.readthedocs.io){target="_blank"} sends the request to the API - [Polars](https://docs.pola.rs){target="_blank"} holds and cleans the results - [python-dotenv](https://pypi.org/project/python-dotenv/){target="_blank"} loads your API key from a file ```bash pip install requests polars python-dotenv ``` ## Store your API key Create a file named `.env` in your project folder. Put one line in it, using your own key: ``` CENSUS_API_KEY=your_key_goes_here ``` Then load it at the top of your script or notebook: ::: {#b32105f0 .cell execution_count=2} ``` {.python .cell-code} import os import polars as pl import requests from dotenv import load_dotenv load_dotenv() API_KEY = os.getenv("CENSUS_API_KEY") ``` ::: `load_dotenv()` looks for `.env` in the folder that holds your script and then in each folder above it. If `API_KEY` comes back as `None`, move `.env` into the same folder as your script or notebook. ::: {.callout-warning} ## Keep `.env` out of Git Add `.env` to your project's `.gitignore` file before you commit anything. Your key should never appear on GitHub. ::: ## Anatomy of a request Every Census API request is a URL. Here is one that asks for median household income in every North Carolina county: ``` https://api.census.gov/data/2024/acs/acs5?get=NAME,B19013_001E,B19013_001M&for=county:*&in=state:37&key=YOUR_KEY ``` It has five parts: | Part | Example | Meaning | |----|----|----| | Year | `2024` | The data vintage. For the 5-year ACS, 2024 means 2020 to 2024. | | Dataset | `acs/acs5` | The ACS 5-year detailed tables. Others include `acs/acs1`, `acs/acs5/subject`, and `dec/dhc`. | | `get` | `NAME,B19013_001E,B19013_001M` | The variables you want, separated by commas | | `for` | `county:*` | The geography level you want. `*` means "all of them." | | `in` | `state:37` | A parent geography that limits the results. `37` is North Carolina's FIPS code. | Try it. Paste the URL into your browser with your key in place of `YOUR_KEY`. You will see rows of text in square brackets. That is the raw JSON response. ::: {.callout-important} ## The API needs FIPS codes tidycensus accepts names like `"Mecklenburg"`. The raw API doesn't. You must use numeric FIPS codes such as `37` for North Carolina and `119` for Mecklenburg County. You will learn how to look them up later in this tutorial. ::: ## Making the request in Python Rather than building the URL by hand, give requests a dictionary of parameters. It assembles the URL and handles any special characters for you: ::: {#0cea0ec8 .cell execution_count=3} ``` {.python .cell-code} url = "https://api.census.gov/data/2024/acs/acs5" params = { "get": "NAME,B19013_001E,B19013_001M", "for": "county:*", "in": "state:37", "key": API_KEY, } response = requests.get(url, params=params) response.status_code ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=2} ``` 200 ``` ::: ::: A status code of `200` usually means success. Now look at the data: ::: {#0238cefb .cell execution_count=4} ``` {.python .cell-code} rows = response.json() rows[:3] ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=3} ``` [['NAME', 'B19013_001E', 'B19013_001M', 'state', 'county'], ['Alamance County, North Carolina', '65651', '1854', '37', '001'], ['Alexander County, North Carolina', '65354', '4962', '37', '003']] ``` ::: ::: The response is a **list of lists**. The first inner list is the header row. Every list after that is one county. ::: {.callout-tip} ## When the key is wrong If your key is missing or invalid, the API still returns status `200`. It sends back an HTML error page instead of data, and `response.json()` fails with a confusing `JSONDecodeError`. When you see that error, check `response.url`. If it ends in `missing_key.html` or `invalid_key.html`, the problem is your key. Remember that you have to activate a new key through the link in your email. ::: ## Loading the results into Polars Pass the header row as the column names and the remaining rows as data: ::: {#4a090297 .cell execution_count=5} ``` {.python .cell-code} nc_income = pl.DataFrame(rows[1:], schema=rows[0], orient="row") nc_income.head() ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=4} ```{=html}
shape: (5, 5)
NAMEB19013_001EB19013_001Mstatecounty
strstrstrstrstr
"Alamance County, North Carolin…"65651""1854""37""001"
"Alexander County, North Caroli…"65354""4962""37""003"
"Alleghany County, North Caroli…"47172""4894""37""005"
"Anson County, North Carolina""47302""5753""37""007"
"Ashe County, North Carolina""56866""4577""37""009"
``` ::: ::: Look at the data types under each column name. **Every column is a string**, including the numbers. The API sends everything as text. Cleaning takes three steps: 1. Convert the estimate and MOE columns to numbers. 2. Build a `GEOID` by pasting the state and county codes together. 3. Give the columns readable names. ::: {#5f32a7b8 .cell execution_count=6} ``` {.python .cell-code} nc_income = ( nc_income .with_columns( pl.col("B19013_001E", "B19013_001M").cast(pl.Float64), pl.concat_str("state", "county").alias("GEOID"), ) .rename({"B19013_001E": "median_income", "B19013_001M": "median_income_moe"}) .select("GEOID", "NAME", "median_income", "median_income_moe") ) nc_income.sort("median_income", descending=True).head(5) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=5} ```{=html}
shape: (5, 4)
GEOIDNAMEmedian_incomemedian_income_moe
strstrf64f64
"37183""Wake County, North Carolina"105768.01626.0
"37179""Union County, North Carolina"102900.01953.0
"37037""Chatham County, North Carolina"94317.04141.0
"37053""Currituck County, North Caroli…93511.08425.0
"37029""Camden County, North Carolina"91078.014321.0
``` ::: ::: Notice that `GEOID` stays a string. That preserves the leading zeros in county codes like `001`. ### Watch for missing value codes The API doesn't send blanks for missing values. It sends large negative numbers such as `-666666666`. Each code has a specific meaning, such as "too few sample cases to compute an estimate." None of them are real values, and they will wreck an average or a color scale if you leave them in. Estimates and MOEs are never negative, so it is safe to turn every negative value into a null: ::: {#437b2560 .cell execution_count=7} ``` {.python .cell-code} nc_income = nc_income.with_columns( pl.when(pl.col(c) < 0).then(None).otherwise(pl.col(c)).alias(c) for c in ["median_income", "median_income_moe"] ) ``` ::: You rarely see these codes at the county level. They are common at the tract level. ## A reusable function You don't want to repeat all of those steps for every request. The function below wraps them up. It takes a dictionary that maps readable names to variable IDs. It returns a clean DataFrame with a `GEOID` column. ::: {#3d680c0a .cell execution_count=8} ``` {.python .cell-code} def get_census(dataset, year, variables, geo_for, geo_in=None): """Request data from the Census API and return a clean Polars DataFrame. variables maps new column names to Census variable IDs, for example {"median_income": "B19013_001E"}. """ url = f"https://api.census.gov/data/{year}/{dataset}" params = { "get": ",".join(["NAME", *variables.values()]), "for": geo_for, "key": API_KEY, } if geo_in is not None: params["in"] = geo_in response = requests.get(url, params=params) if response.status_code != 200: raise ValueError(f"Census API error: {response.text}") if response.url.endswith("_key.html"): raise ValueError(f"Problem with your API key. See {response.url}") rows = response.json() df = pl.DataFrame(rows[1:], schema=rows[0], orient="row") # Geography columns (state, county, tract, ...) come after the variables geo_cols = df.columns[len(variables) + 1:] new_names = list(variables.keys()) return ( df .rename(dict(zip(variables.values(), new_names))) .with_columns( pl.col(new_names).cast(pl.Float64), pl.concat_str(geo_cols).alias("GEOID"), ) .with_columns( pl.when(pl.col(c) < 0).then(None).otherwise(pl.col(c)).alias(c) for c in new_names ) .select("GEOID", "NAME", *new_names) ) ``` ::: Now the request from earlier takes only a few lines: ::: {#88f6c4c5 .cell execution_count=9} ``` {.python .cell-code} nc_income = get_census( dataset="acs/acs5", year=2024, variables={ "median_income": "B19013_001E", "median_income_moe": "B19013_001M", }, geo_for="county:*", geo_in="state:37", ) ``` ::: ::: {.callout-tip} ## Save the function for later Copy `get_census()`, together with the import and API key lines above it, into a file named `census_helpers.py` in your project folder. Part 2 imports it with `from census_helpers import get_census`. ::: ## Several variables at once Add more entries to the dictionary. One API request can hold up to 50 variables. ::: {#2a9ab39a .cell execution_count=10} ``` {.python .cell-code} nc_profile = get_census( dataset="acs/acs5", year=2024, variables={ "median_income": "B19013_001E", "median_age": "B01002_001E", "total_pop": "B01003_001E", }, geo_for="county:*", geo_in="state:37", ) ``` ::: This returns one row per county with one column per variable. That is what tidycensus calls "wide" format. ## Finding variables There are two good ways to find variable IDs. **Browse in your browser.** Every dataset has a searchable list of its variables. For the 2024 ACS 5-year, it lives at {target="_blank"}. The page is very large, so use your browser's find feature (Ctrl+F or Cmd+F). **Search with Polars.** The same list is available as JSON. Load it into a DataFrame and filter it: ::: {#daae6fc9 .cell execution_count=11} ``` {.python .cell-code} meta = requests.get("https://api.census.gov/data/2024/acs/acs5/variables.json").json() acs_vars = pl.DataFrame( [ {"name": name, "label": info["label"], "concept": info.get("concept")} for name, info in meta["variables"].items() ] ) ( acs_vars .filter(pl.col("concept").str.contains("(?i)median household income")) .sort("name") .head(12) ) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=10} ```{=html}

"B19013A_001E""Estimate!!Median household inc…"Median Household Income in the…
"B19013B_001E""Estimate!!Median household inc…"Median Household Income in the…
"B19013C_001E""Estimate!!Median household inc…"Median Household Income in the…

"B19013H_001E""Estimate!!Median household inc…"Median Household Income in the…
"B19013I_001E""Estimate!!Median household inc…"Median Household Income in the…

"B19019_001E""Estimate!!Total:""Median Household Income in the…

``` ::: ::: The `(?i)` at the start of the pattern makes the search ignore case. Look closely at the results. You will see `B19013_001E` along with `B19013A_001E` through `B19013I_001E`. The lettered versions repeat the table for specific racial and ethnic groups. For example, `B19013B` covers households headed by someone who is Black alone. Tables with `PR` in the ID cover Puerto Rico only. Labels use `!!` to separate the levels of a table. The first row of most tables (the variable ending in `_001E`) is the total for that table. You will often use it as a denominator. If you already know the table you want, the `groups` endpoint lists just its variables. Try {target="_blank"}. ## Computing percentages and their MOEs Table `B17001` counts people by poverty status. `B17001_002E` is the number of people below the poverty level. `B17001_001E` is the number of people for whom poverty status is determined. Divide one by the other to get a rate: ::: {#568760fc .cell execution_count=12} ``` {.python .cell-code} nc_poverty = get_census( dataset="acs/acs5", year=2024, variables={ "below_poverty": "B17001_002E", "below_poverty_moe": "B17001_002M", "universe": "B17001_001E", "universe_moe": "B17001_001M", }, geo_for="county:*", geo_in="state:37", ) ``` ::: A derived number needs a derived margin of error. The Census Bureau publishes a formula for the MOE of a proportion. The code below follows it. It uses a fallback formula when the value under the square root would be negative. This is the same calculation that tidycensus performs with `moe_prop()`. ::: {#ce5a50c9 .cell execution_count=13} ``` {.python .cell-code} p = pl.col("below_poverty") / pl.col("universe") under_root = pl.col("below_poverty_moe") ** 2 - p**2 * pl.col("universe_moe") ** 2 fallback = pl.col("below_poverty_moe") ** 2 + p**2 * pl.col("universe_moe") ** 2 nc_poverty = nc_poverty.with_columns( (100 * p).alias("pct_poverty"), ( 100 * pl.when(under_root < 0).then(fallback).otherwise(under_root).sqrt() / pl.col("universe") ).alias("pct_poverty_moe"), ) nc_poverty.select("NAME", "pct_poverty", "pct_poverty_moe").sort( "pct_poverty", descending=True ) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=12} ```{=html}

``` ::: ::: ## Going smaller: census tracts For tracts, set `geo_for` to `tract:*`. Then limit the results with a state and a county in `geo_in`, separated by a space. Mecklenburg County's FIPS code is `119`: ::: {#76012599 .cell execution_count=14} ``` {.python .cell-code} meck_income = get_census( dataset="acs/acs5", year=2024, variables={ "median_income": "B19013_001E", "median_income_moe": "B19013_001M", }, geo_for="tract:*", geo_in="state:37 county:119", ) meck_income.height ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=13} ``` 305 ``` ::: ::: You should get 305 tracts. The GEOIDs are now 11 digits long. The function pastes together the state, county, and tract codes for you. ### Looking up county FIPS codes To find a county's code, request the list of counties. You only need the `NAME` variable, so pass an empty dictionary: ::: {#dc534e0b .cell execution_count=15} ``` {.python .cell-code} nc_counties = get_census("acs/acs5", 2024, {}, "county:*", "state:37") nc_counties.filter(pl.col("NAME").str.contains("Iredell|Cabarrus")) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=14} ```{=html}
shape: (2, 2)

"37025""Cabarrus County, North Carolin…
"37097""Iredell County, North Carolina"
``` ::: ::: The last three digits of each GEOID are the county code. Iredell is `097` and Cabarrus is `025`. You can request tracts from several counties at once by separating their codes with commas: ::: {#94e18601 .cell execution_count=16} ``` {.python .cell-code} lkn_income = get_census( dataset="acs/acs5", year=2024, variables={"median_income": "B19013_001E", "median_income_moe": "B19013_001M"}, geo_for="tract:*", geo_in="state:37 county:119,097,025", ) ``` ::: ### Watch the margins of error Tract estimates rest on small samples. Compare each MOE to its estimate to find the shaky ones: ::: {#0b1ef2d2 .cell execution_count=17} ``` {.python .cell-code} ( meck_income .with_columns((pl.col("median_income_moe") / pl.col("median_income")).alias("moe_ratio")) .sort("moe_ratio", descending=True, nulls_last=True) .head(10) ) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=16} ```{=html}

``` ::: ::: Also count how many tracts have null estimates with `meck_income["median_income"].null_count()`. In Mecklenburg, the nulls are tracts 9801, 9802, and 9803. Tracts numbered in the 9800s are *special land-use tracts* that cover places like airports and large parks. Few or no people live in them, so the Bureau can't compute an income. ::: {.callout-tip} ## Top-coded values Sort `meck_income` by `median_income` from highest to lowest and look at the top tract. Its estimate is exactly `250001`, and its MOE is null. That isn't a real income. The ACS *top-codes* medians, so `250001` means "$250,000 or more." Keep this in mind if you average incomes or rank the wealthiest tracts. ::: ## The 2020 decennial census The decennial census uses the same function with a different dataset name. Decennial variable IDs end in `N` because they are counts, and they have no MOEs. Total population by county, from the Demographic and Housing Characteristics file: ::: {#d5c35338 .cell execution_count=18} ``` {.python .cell-code} nc_pop_2020 = get_census( dataset="dec/dhc", year=2020, variables={"total_pop": "P1_001N"}, geo_for="county:*", geo_in="state:37", ) ``` ::: The Redistricting file (`dec/pl`) has race and ethnicity counts. Here is the share of each Mecklenburg tract's population that identifies as Black alone: ::: {#6addb6ac .cell execution_count=19} ``` {.python .cell-code} meck_black = get_census( dataset="dec/pl", year=2020, variables={"black_alone": "P1_004N", "total_pop": "P1_001N"}, geo_for="tract:*", geo_in="state:37 county:119", ).with_columns( (100 * pl.col("black_alone") / pl.col("total_pop")).alias("pct_black") ) ``` ::: You can browse decennial variables at {target="_blank"} and {target="_blank"}. ## Saving your data ::: {#b94c5222 .cell execution_count=20} ``` {.python .cell-code} nc_poverty.write_csv("nc_poverty_2024.csv") ``` ::: When you read the file back, tell Polars that `GEOID` is text. Otherwise it will guess that the column is a number and drop leading zeros: ::: {#7954d68b .cell execution_count=21} ``` {.python .cell-code} nc_poverty = pl.read_csv("nc_poverty_2024.csv", schema_overrides={"GEOID": pl.String}) ``` ::: ## Try it yourself 1. Find the variable for median gross rent. Pull it for every North Carolina county. Which five counties have the highest rent? 2. Compute the percentage of households in each Mecklenburg tract that have no vehicle available, along with its MOE. Table `B08201` is a good place to start. 3. The API also offers the ACS subject tables at `acs/acs5/subject`. Subject tables often include percentages that are already computed. Find the poverty rate in table `S1701` and compare it to your own calculation. ## Further reading - The Census Bureau's [API user guide](https://www.census.gov/data/developers/guidance/api-user-guide.html){target="_blank"} and [list of example queries](https://www.census.gov/data/developers/guidance/api-user-guide.Example_API_Queries.html){target="_blank"} - Kyle Walker's [*Analyzing US Census Data*](https://walker-data.com/census-r/){target="_blank"} is written for R. The ideas in [Chapter 2](https://walker-data.com/census-r/an-introduction-to-tidycensus.html){target="_blank"} and [Chapter 3](https://walker-data.com/census-r/wrangling-census-data-with-tidyverse-tools.html){target="_blank"} carry over directly, especially the discussion of margins of error. **Next:** [Census Data in Python, Part 2: Mapping](census-python-part2.qmd)
